# p-values {#p-values}

<div class="draft">Work in progress.</div>

- In Chapter \@ref(null-distributions) we took 1000 groups of 10 Steves from a world where Steves are average, worked out a t-value for each, and found cutoffs that leave the most extreme 5% outside
- Here we put a number on how rare a t-value is: the share of null t-values beyond it
- That share is the **p-value**: the probability of a result at least as extreme as ours if the null hypothesis is true
- Then we simulate p-values with and without a real effect, to see what they can and can't tell us

<div class="summary-box">
null t-values -> share at least as extreme as ours -> p-value
</div>

<div class="note">
**What you need for this chapter**

- Chapter \@ref(standard-error-t) (`my_t_value()`) and Chapter \@ref(null-distributions) (`my_null_t()`, `my_cutoffs()`)
</div>

```{r toolbox-check}
all.equal(my_t_value(scores, 49), unname(t.test(scores, mu = 49)$statistic))

set.seed(1)
mine <- my_null_t(n = 10, pop_mean = 175, pop_sd = 7)

  t.test(rnorm(n = 10, mean = 175, sd = 7), mu = 175)$statistic
)
all.equal(mine, r_version)

all.equal(my_cutoffs(20:1, alpha = 0.1), c(2, 19))

- Rebuild `null_ts` from Chapter \@ref(null-distributions): 1000 null t-values from groups of 10 Steves
- `map_dbl(1:1000, \(i) ...)` runs the code 1000 times and keeps each number

```{r null-ts}
set.seed(10)
null_ts <- map_dbl(1:1000, \(i) my_null_t(n = 10, pop_mean = 175, pop_sd = 7))
cutoffs <- my_cutoffs(null_ts)
cutoffs
```

## Alpha And Type I Errors

- All 1000 `null_ts` come from a world where the null is true
- If we call a result "far" when it's past `cutoffs`, we're wrong for the 5% past them
- Calling a result "far" when nothing is going on is a **Type I error**
- In the last chapter alpha was the share of null values we marked as rare. It's also the probability of a Type I error
- With alpha = .05, the test makes a Type I error 5% of the time when the null is true

```{r type-i-plot, fig.cap="The 1000 null t-values. The ones past the cutoffs (orange) would be Type I errors.", fig.alt="Histogram of 1000 t-values centred on zero. Bars beyond two dashed cutoff lines near -2.3 and 2.3 are orange; the rest are blue.", echo=FALSE}
tibble(t = null_ts) |>
  mutate(past = t < cutoffs[1] | t > cutoffs[2]) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = t, fill = past)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, boundary = 0, colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = cutoffs, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_manual(NULL, values = c(`FALSE` = "#467AAC", `TRUE` = "#D55E00"),
                    labels = c("Not past the cutoffs", "Past the cutoffs: Type I error")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-6, 6)) +
  labs(x = "t-value", y = "Count") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r type-i-plot-code, ref.label="type-i-plot", eval=FALSE, webex.hide="Show the plot code"}
```

- Count them:

```{r type-i-count}
past <- null_ts < cutoffs[1] | null_ts > cutoffs[2]
sum(past)
my_mean(past)
```

<iframe class="demyst-widget" src="apps/nhst/embed.html?mode=null&n=10&null=175&sd=7&unit=cm" width="100%" height="760" title="Null distribution of t interactive widget" style="border: 0;"></iframe>

1. Click **+1** a few times, then **+1000**. The share past the cutoffs settles near 5%, the Type I error rate
2. Set **Show t-values as** to **Dots**. The solid dots are the samples wrongly called "far"

## Your Turn: Write `my_sim_p_value()`

- This answers "how far is far enough?" from Chapter \@ref(null-distributions)
- The p-value is the proportion of null t-values at least as far from zero as ours

$$
p = \frac{\text{number of null t-values with } |t_{\text{null}}| \geq |t|}{\text{number of null t-values}}
$$

- $|t|$ is the **absolute value**, the distance from zero with the sign dropped (`abs()` in R)
- Steps:
  1. for each null t-value: `abs(null_ts) >= abs(t)`
  2. proportion of `TRUE`s
- The proportion of `TRUE`s is the mean of the TRUE/FALSE values (TRUE counts as 1, FALSE as 0), so `my_mean()` does it

```{r my-sim-p-value-exercise, eval=FALSE}
my_sim_p_value <- function(t, null_ts) {
  as_extreme <-
  output <-
  return(output)
}

my_sim_p_value(t = 0.95, null_ts = null_ts)
```

`r hide("Show a hint")`
`as_extreme` is `abs(null_ts) >= abs(t)`, and `output` is `my_mean(as_extreme)`.
`r unhide()`

`r hide("Show one solution")`
```{r my-sim-p-value-solution}
my_sim_p_value <- function(t, null_ts) {
  as_extreme <- abs(null_ts) >= abs(t)
  output <- my_mean(as_extreme)
  return(output)
}

my_sim_p_value(t = 0.95, null_ts = null_ts)
```
`r unhide()`

- `abs()` makes both tails count, so -3 is as far out as 3. This is a **two-sided** p-value

```{r sim-p-plot, fig.cap="The simulated p-value for t = 0.95: the share of null t-values at least as far from zero (orange).", fig.alt="Histogram of null t-values. Bars below -0.95 and above 0.95 are orange, the middle is blue. Solid lines mark -0.95 and 0.95.", echo=FALSE}
tibble(t = null_ts) |>
  mutate(as_extreme = abs(t) >= 0.95) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = t, fill = as_extreme)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, boundary = 0.95, colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-0.95, 0.95), linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_fill_manual(NULL, values = c(`FALSE` = "#467AAC", `TRUE` = "#D55E00"),
                    labels = c("Closer to zero", "At least as far out as 0.95")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-6, 6)) +
  labs(x = "t-value", y = "Count") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r sim-p-plot-code, ref.label="sim-p-plot", eval=FALSE, webex.hide="Show the plot code"}
```

## Check It: Close Enough

- Back to the ten scores from Chapter \@ref(standard-error-t), against comparison values 49 and 46
- The Steve null t-values still work here: under the null, the distribution of t depends only on the sample size, not the mean or SD
- With 1000 samples the simulated p wobbles around the exact one, so `all.equal()` would fail
- Instead we check the gap is small: `abs(...) < 0.05`

```{r sim-p-check}
t_49 <- my_t_value(scores, comparison_value = 49)

c(
  simulated = my_sim_p_value(t_49, null_ts),
  R = t.test(scores, mu = 49)$p.value
)
abs(my_sim_p_value(t_49, null_ts) - t.test(scores, mu = 49)$p.value) < 0.05
```

```{r sim-p-check-46}
t_46 <- my_t_value(scores, comparison_value = 46)

c(
  simulated = my_sim_p_value(t_46, null_ts),
  R = t.test(scores, mu = 46)$p.value
)
abs(my_sim_p_value(t_46, null_ts) - t.test(scores, mu = 46)$p.value) < 0.05
```

- `TRUE` both times, so the p-values from our own null distribution are within 0.05 of R's

## From Simulation To The t Distribution

- With more and more samples the histogram gets smoother and becomes a curve, the **t distribution**
- Its shape depends only on the degrees of freedom (df = n - 1 = 9 here)

```{r t-curve, fig.cap="The simulated null t-values with the exact t distribution for 9 degrees of freedom drawn over them.", fig.alt="Histogram of simulated t-values with a smooth orange t distribution curve following its shape closely.", echo=FALSE}
curve_data <- tibble(t = seq(-6, 6, 0.05)) |>
  mutate(count = 1000 * 0.25 * dt(t, df = 9))

ggplot(tibble(t = null_ts), aes(x = t)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, boundary = 0, colour = "white", fill = "#467AAC",
                 alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(data = curve_data, aes(x = t, y = count), colour = "#D55E00",
            linewidth = 1.1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-6, 6)) +
  labs(x = "t-value", y = "Count")
```

```{r t-curve-code, ref.label="t-curve", eval=FALSE, webex.hide="Show the plot code"}
```

- R knows this curve exactly, so we don't need to simulate
- `pt()` gives the area below a value. `pt(-2, df = 9)` is the proportion of t-values below -2
- Treat `pt()` like `sum()`: a built-in we use without building it by hand

```{r pt-example}
pt(-2, df = 9)
my_mean(null_ts < -2)
```

## Your Turn: Write `my_p_value()`

$$
p = 2 \times \underbrace{P(T \leq -|t|)}_{\text{area in one tail: } \texttt{pt(-abs(t), df)}}
$$

- Steps:
  1. lower-tail area beyond negative version of our t: `pt(-abs(t), df)`
  2. double it (two-sided; the curve is symmetric)
- `-abs(t)` is always negative, so this works whether t is above or below zero

```{r my-p-value-exercise, eval=FALSE}
my_p_value <- function(t, df) {
  lower_tail <-
  output <-
  return(output)
}

my_p_value(t = 0.95, df = 9)
```

`r hide("Show a hint")`
`lower_tail` is `pt(-abs(t), df)`, and `output` is two times `lower_tail`.
`r unhide()`

`r hide("Show one solution")`
```{r my-p-value-solution}
my_p_value <- function(t, df) {
  lower_tail <- pt(-abs(t), df)
  output <- 2 * lower_tail
  return(output)
}

my_p_value(t = 0.95, df = 9)
```
`r unhide()`

## Check It Against `t.test()`

- No simulation this time, so the match should be exact

```{r my-p-value-check}
c(mine = my_p_value(t_49, df = 9), R = t.test(scores, mu = 49)$p.value)
all.equal(my_p_value(t_49, df = 9), t.test(scores, mu = 49)$p.value)

all.equal(my_p_value(t_46, df = 9), t.test(scores, mu = 46)$p.value)
```

## Back To Our Two Comparison Values

```{r p-values, echo=FALSE}
p_49 <- my_p_value(t_49, df = 9)
p_46 <- my_p_value(t_46, df = 9)
sim_49 <- my_sim_p_value(t_49, null_ts)
sim_46 <- my_sim_p_value(t_46, null_ts)
```

| Comparison value | t | Simulated p | Exact p | Past the cutoff at alpha .05? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 49 | `r round(t_49, 2)` | `r round(sim_49, 3)` | `r round(p_49, 3)` | No |
| 46 | `r round(t_46, 2)` | `r round(sim_46, 3)` | `r round(p_46, 3)` | Yes |

- Against 49, a t this far out turns up in about `r round(100 * p_49)`% of null samples. Not unusual, so we don't reject the null
  - This doesn't show the mean is 49, only that the data are compatible with it
- Against 46, it turns up in under 1% of null samples. It's past the cutoff, so we reject the null that the mean is 46
- p below alpha and t past the cutoffs are the same decision

## Misreading p-Values

- A p-value is the probability of a result this extreme if the null is true. It isn't the probability that the null is true
- Simulating p-values in two worlds shows what they can and can't tell us

### In A World With No Effect

- 1000 groups of 10 average Steves, one p-value each (from `null_ts`)

```{r null-ps}
null_ps <- my_p_value(null_ts, df = 9)
my_mean(null_ps < 0.05)
```

```{r null-ps-plot, fig.cap="p-values from 1000 groups in a world with no effect. Every value from 0 to 1 is about equally common.", fig.alt="Histogram of 1000 p-values from 0 to 1 in bins of 0.05. The bars are roughly flat at about 50 each; the first bar, below .05, is orange.", echo=FALSE}
tibble(p = null_ps) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = p, fill = p < 0.05)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05, boundary = 0, colour = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(NULL, values = c(`FALSE` = "#467AAC", `TRUE` = "#D55E00"),
                    labels = c("p of .05 or more", "p below .05")) +
  labs(x = "p-value", y = "Count") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r null-ps-plot-code, ref.label="null-ps-plot", eval=FALSE, webex.hide="Show the plot code"}
```

- The histogram is flat. When the null is true, p = .80 and p = .03 are equally likely
- About 5% fall below .05, which is alpha again
- So a large p isn't evidence for the null. With no effect, p is just a random number between 0 and 1

### In A World With An Effect

- Now Steves really are taller: mean 180 cm, SD 7, still compared with 175
- Run the same study 20 times with groups of 10

```{r effect-ps}
set.seed(4)
effect_ps <- map_dbl(1:20, \(i) {
  steves <- rnorm(n = 10, mean = 180, sd = 7)
  my_p_value(my_t_value(steves, comparison_value = 175), df = 9)
})
round(sort(effect_ps), 3)
my_mean(effect_ps < 0.05)
```

```{r effect-ps-plot, fig.cap="p-values from 20 identical studies in a world where Steves really are 5 cm taller.", fig.alt="Dot plot of 20 p-values, one per study, on a scale from 0 to 1. Orange dots below the dashed line at .05, blue dots spread above it, up to about 0.5.", echo=FALSE, fig.height=5}
tibble(study = 1:20, p = effect_ps) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = p, y = factor(study), colour = p < 0.05)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(NULL, values = c(`FALSE` = "#467AAC", `TRUE` = "#D55E00"),
                      labels = c("p of .05 or more", "p below .05")) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "p-value", y = "Study") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r effect-ps-plot-code, ref.label="effect-ps-plot", eval=FALSE, webex.hide="Show the plot code"}
```

- Same world, same design, and p-values from below .001 to almost .5
- `r sum(effect_ps >= 0.05)` of the 20 studies miss a real 5 cm difference
- What this means:
  - p above .05 doesn't mean there's no effect
  - p doesn't tell you how big an effect is
  - one study's p is a noisy draw. How often it falls below .05 depends on the effect and the sample size, which is **power** (Chapter \@ref(power))
- The exact p from `t.test()` assumes independent observations from a normal population. Our simulation assumed the same, through `rnorm()`

Which statement describes a p-value of .004? `r mcq(c("There is a 0.4% chance that the null hypothesis is true", answer = "If the null hypothesis were true, a t-value at least this extreme would turn up in about 0.4% of samples", "There is a 99.6% chance that there is a real difference"))`

A study finds p = .40. What can you conclude? `r mcq(c("There is no effect", "The null hypothesis is 40% likely to be true", answer = "A result this extreme is common when there is no effect, so the study gives no good reason to reject the null"))`

## Try It On Real Data

- The `sleep` data: extra hours of sleep on the first drug for 10 patients, compared with 0 (no extra sleep)
- 10 patients, so `null_ts` works here

```{r real-data-p}
drug_1 <- sleep |> filter(group == 1) |> pull(extra)
drug_t <- my_t_value(drug_1, comparison_value = 0)

c(
  simulated = my_sim_p_value(drug_t, null_ts),
  exact = my_p_value(drug_t, df = 9),
  R = t.test(drug_1, mu = 0)$p.value
)

abs(my_sim_p_value(drug_t, null_ts) - t.test(drug_1, mu = 0)$p.value) < 0.05
all.equal(my_p_value(drug_t, df = 9), t.test(drug_1, mu = 0)$p.value)
```

- `null_ts` came from heights (mean 175, SD 7), not sleep. That's fine because the null distribution of t depends only on the sample size
- p is about `r round(my_p_value(drug_t, df = 9), 2)`, not below .05, so we don't reject "no extra sleep"
- That doesn't show the drug does nothing. With 10 patients a modest effect is easy to miss

# p-values -----------------------------------------------------------------
my_sim_p_value <- function(t, null_ts) {
  as_extreme <- abs(null_ts) >= abs(t)
  output <- my_mean(as_extreme)
  return(output)
}

my_p_value <- function(t, df) {
  lower_tail <- pt(-abs(t), df)
  output <- 2 * lower_tail
  return(output)
}
```
